# Chapter 6: Designing a Personal Dashboard

Imagine opening Notion and immediately knowing exactly what to work on. No clicking through five different pages in your sidebar, no scrolling through a long list of notes trying to find the project you started last week, and no wondering if you’ve forgotten a deadline. Instead, you land on a single, central hub where your most urgent tasks, your daily notes, and your quick links all live together in one organized view. 

This is the power of a personal dashboard. 

Up to this point in the book, you’ve learned how to build individual pages, format text blocks, create databases, customize views, and automate repetitive actions with templates and buttons. You have all the building blocks. Now, it’s time to assemble them into a unified command center. 

## What is a Personal Dashboard?

In Notion, a dashboard is simply a standard page, but it is designed with a specific purpose: to act as your home base. Instead of being a destination for deep work or long-form writing, a dashboard is a launchpad. It surfaces the information you need to see every day and provides quick links to the systems you manage behind the scenes.

Think of it like the dashboard of a car. You don’t look at the speedometer to learn how the engine works; you look at it to see how fast you are going right now. Similarly, your Notion dashboard doesn't hold every task you've ever been assigned. Instead, it holds a *linked view* of your tasks that are due today. 

By consolidating your workflows into a central home page, you save time, reduce friction, and ensure that nothing important slips through the cracks.

## Creating Your Home Base Page

Before we can style your dashboard or pull in your tasks, we need to create the page itself. 

1. In your **sidebar**, navigate to your **Private** section (or your main workspace area).
2. Click the **+** icon next to a section to create a new **page**.
3. When the blank page appears, click the title area and name it "Dashboard" or "Home Base."
4. Because you will be visiting this page constantly, add it to your **Favorites** in the sidebar. You can do this by hovering over the page name in the sidebar, clicking the **•••** icon, and selecting **Add to Favorites**. Alternatively, you can click the **•••** icon in the top right of the page itself and choose **Favorite**.

Now, whenever you open Notion, this page will be waiting for you in the Favorites section at the top of your sidebar. 

## Improving Visual Navigation

A wall of text is difficult to scan. To make your dashboard truly function as a command center, you need to use visual cues that help your brain process information faster. Notion provides three primary tools for this: icons, cover images, and columns.

### Adding Icons and Cover Images

When you create a new page, you might notice the placeholder options at the very top: "Add icon" and "Add cover". 

*   **Icons:** An icon is a small image or emoji that appears in the top left corner of the page, next to the title. In the sidebar, this icon acts as a visual bookmark, making it much faster to locate your Dashboard among your other pages. To add one, click "Add icon," then click the generated emoji to browse hundreds of options, upload a custom image, or search the web for a specific logo or graphic.
*   **Cover Images:** A cover image is a wide banner that stretches across the top of your page, above the title. Covers set the aesthetic tone for your dashboard. Click "Add cover" to generate a random Unsplash image. If you click the image, you'll get options to "Change cover," where you can upload your own photo, paste an image link, or search a built-in gallery of free-to-use photos. 

For a dashboard, choose an icon that feels universally recognizable to you (like a house, a compass, or a star) and a cover image that is visually calming or inspiring, so you don't mind looking at it every day.

### Using Columns for Layout

By default, Notion places every block vertically, one on top of the other. If you add a to-do list, a database, and a note, they will stack down the page, requiring you to scroll endlessly. Columns allow you to place blocks side-by-side, fundamentally changing how you use screen space.

Creating columns in Notion relies on a simple drag-and-drop mechanic:

1. Create your first block (for example, type `/heading` and write "Today's Tasks").
2. Hover your mouse over the left side of that block until you see the **drag handle** (a grid of six dots).
3. Click and hold the drag handle, then slowly drag the block to the right side of another block.
4. As you drag, you will see a **blue vertical line** appear. This blue line indicates that you are creating a new column. 
5. Release your mouse click, and the two blocks will now sit side-by-side.

You can adjust the width of these columns by hovering your mouse over the space between them until your cursor turns into a double-sided arrow. Click and drag left or right to resize the columns to your liking. 

## Surfacing Information with Linked Databases

If your dashboard is going to be a true command center, it needs to show you your tasks, projects, or notes. However, you shouldn't create brand new databases on your dashboard. If you do, you'll end up with isolated lists that don't connect to the rest of your workspace. 

Instead, you will use a **linked database**.

### What is a Linked Database?

A linked database is a window into an existing database. It does not duplicate your data. If you add a task to a linked database on your dashboard, that task is instantly added to the original master database. If you check a box on the master database, it appears checked on your dashboard. 

Think of it like a security camera feed. You can have multiple monitors (linked databases) showing different angles of the same room (the master database), but there is only one actual room. Changing something on the monitor changes it in the room, because they are one and the same.

### Creating Your First Linked Database

Let's assume you already have a master Task database created from our earlier chapter on Introduction to Databases. To surface those tasks on your dashboard:

1. On your Dashboard page, type `/linked view of a database` (or simply type `/linked` and select it from the menu).
2. A search bar will appear. Start typing the name of your master database (e.g., "Task List").
3. Select the database from the dropdown list. 
4. Notion will immediately drop a view of that database onto your page. 

By default, this linked view will look exactly like the default view of your master database. But the whole point of a dashboard is to show you only what matters *right now*. 

### Filtering for Relevance

You likely don't want to see every task you've ever created on your home base. You only want to see what is due today, or what is currently in progress. Because we covered Customizing Database Views in a previous chapter, you already know how to manipulate this data. 

To make your linked database useful:

1. Click the **•••** icon in the top right of your linked database.
2. Select **Filter**.
3. Add a filter based on a property in your database. For example, if you have a "Status" property, you might filter for "In Progress." If you have a "Due Date" property, you might filter for "Today."
4. Rename the view by clicking the default name (usually "Table view") at the top left of the database. Rename it to something like "Action Items" or "Today's Tasks."

Now, your dashboard is only surfacing the specific slice of information you need to act on today, while the master database safely stores the rest of your tasks in the background.

## Putting It All Together: A Dashboard Walkthrough

Let’s look at a concrete scenario to see how these elements combine into a functional layout. 

Meet Alex. Alex is a freelance graphic designer who uses Notion to manage client projects, daily tasks, and meeting notes. Alex wants a dashboard that separates work into clear zones. 

Here is how Alex structures the dashboard using columns and linked databases:

**The Top Zone: Quick Capture**
At the very top of the page, Alex places a simple text block: *"What's the main focus for today?"* Beneath it, Alex adds a **Button** (covered in our previous module). The button is configured to say "Log a quick thought." When clicked, it adds a new entry to a master "Brain Dump" database. This ensures that when Alex opens the dashboard and suddenly remembers an email he needs to send, he can capture it in two seconds without navigating away from the home base.

**The Middle Zone: The Split View**
This is where Alex uses columns to divide the screen.
*   **Left Column (70% width):** Alex creates a linked view of his "Client Projects" database. He applies a filter so this view only shows projects where the Status is "Active." He changes the view type to a **Board** (Kanban style), so he can drag and drop projects between "To Do," "In Review," and "Completed" directly from the dashboard.
*   **Right Column (30% width):** Alex creates a second linked view, this time of his "Task List" database. He filters this view to only show tasks where the "Due Date" is "Today." He leaves this as a **List** view so he can easily check the checkboxes next to each task as he completes them throughout the day.

**The Bottom Zone: Quick Links**
At the bottom of the page, Alex doesn't want to clutter the screen with more databases. Instead, he wants quick access to his reference materials. He types `/link to page` and selects his "Meeting Notes" page, and does it again for his "Invoices" database. These appear as clickable text links, acting like a bookmark bar at the bottom of his dashboard.

By structuring the page this way, Alex has consolidated his entire workflow into a single screen. He can see his big-picture projects on the left, his granular tasks on the right, capture passing thoughts at the top, and jump to his archives at the bottom. 

## A Note on Iteration

When you build your first dashboard, it is highly unlikely that it will be perfect on day one. You might add a linked database for your reading list, only to realize a week later that you don't actually need to see your reading list every single time you open Notion. 

That is completely normal. A dashboard is a living document. 

If a section feels cluttered, remove it. If you find yourself clicking into the same page every morning, add a quick link to it on your dashboard. If a column feels too narrow, drag the edge to widen it. The flexibility of blocks, columns, and linked databases means your home base can evolve right alongside your organizational needs. 

## Key Takeaways

*   A **dashboard** is a standard Notion page designed to act as your home base, surfacing daily priorities and linking to deeper workflows.
*   Add the dashboard to your **Favorites** in the sidebar so it is instantly accessible every time you open your workspace.
*   Use **icons** and **cover images** to give your dashboard a distinct visual identity, making it easy to spot in your sidebar.
*   **Columns** are created by dragging a block's handle to the right of another block until a blue vertical line appears. Columns prevent endless vertical scrolling and allow for side-by-side layouts.
*   A **linked database** is a live window into an existing master database. It does not duplicate data; any changes made in the linked view update the master database, and vice versa.
*   Use **filters** on your linked databases to ensure your dashboard only surfaces highly relevant information (like tasks due today), keeping the view clean and focused.

## 1. A Task Management System That Works for You  

### 1.1 Create the “Tasks” database  

1. From your **Personal Dashboard** (see chapter *Designing a Personal Dashboard*), click the **+ New** button at the bottom of the page.  
2. Choose **Database → Table – Full page** and name it **Tasks**.  
3. Press **Enter** to create the database. Notion automatically adds a **Name** column—this will be the task title.

### 1.2 Add essential properties  

| Property | Type | Why it matters |
|----------|------|----------------|
| **Priority** | **Select** (High, Medium, Low) | Lets you spot urgent work at a glance. |
| **Due Date** | **Date** | Enables calendar‑based planning. |
| **Status** | **Select** (To‑Do, In Progress, Done) | Tracks progress without opening each page. |
| **Project** | **Select** (Project A, Project B, Personal) | Groups tasks by the larger goal they serve. |

To add a property, click the **+** button next to the last column, select the appropriate type, and give it the name above. Remember the **Select** type (introduced in *Introduction to Databases*) lets you choose from a predefined list, while **Date** lets you pick a calendar day.

### 1.3 Build useful views  

A **view** is a filtered, sorted, or formatted snapshot of your database (see *Customizing Database Views*). Create three views that will sit on your dashboard:

1. **Today** – Shows only tasks due today.  
   - Click **Add a view**, select **Table**, name it *Today*, and hit **Create**.  
   - Click **Filter** → **Add a filter** → **Due Date** → **Is today**.  
   - Sort by **Priority** (High → Low) so the most critical items appear first.

2. **Upcoming** – Displays the next 7 days.  
   - New view → **Table** → *Upcoming*.  
   - Filter: **Due Date** → **Is within the next** → **7** days.  
   - Sort by **Due Date** (earliest → latest).

3. **By Priority** – Groups tasks by their priority regardless of date.  
   - New view → **Board** (Kanban style) → *By Priority*.  
   - Group by **Priority**.  
   - Drag cards between columns to change a task’s priority instantly.

### 1.4 Speed up entry with a template  

Using **Templates** (chapter *Using Templates and Buttons for Efficiency*) lets you pre‑fill common fields:

1. Inside the **Tasks** database, click **New** → **+ New template**.  
2. Name the template **Standard Task**.  
3. Fill in default values:  
   - **Priority** → *Medium*  
   - **Status** → *To‑Do*  
   - **Project** → *Personal*  
4. Add a **checkbox** block titled **Follow‑up needed?** – this can be a quick reminder for tasks that require a later check‑in.  
5. Click **Close**.  

Now every time you click **New → Standard Task**, those fields are already set, saving you typing.

### 1.5 One‑click task creation with a button  

A **Button** (covered in *Using Templates and Buttons for Efficiency*) can be placed on your dashboard to add a fresh task without opening the full database:

1. Go to your **Personal Dashboard**.  
2. Type “/**button**” and select **Button**.  
3. Configure:  
   - **Name**: *Add Quick Task*  
   - **Action**: **Create new page** in **Tasks** database.  
   - **Template**: *Standard Task* (the one you just made).  
4. Click **Done**.  

Pressing this button instantly spawns a new task entry, ready for you to type the title and adjust dates.

## 2. Tracking Daily Habits with a Simple Database  

### 2.1 Why a database beats a plain checklist  

A static checklist can’t show you trends over weeks or months. By storing each habit entry as a row, you can later visualize streaks, filter missed days, or export data for deeper analysis.

### 2.2 Set up the “Habit Tracker” database  

1. From the dashboard, click **+ New → Database → Table – Full page** and name it **Habit Tracker**.  
2. Add the following properties:

| Property | Type | Explanation |
|----------|------|-------------|
| **Habit** | **Select** (e.g., Meditate, Exercise, Read) | The habit you’re tracking. |
| **Date** | **Date** | The day the habit was performed. |
| **Completed** | **Checkbox** | Tick when you finish the habit. |
| **Notes** | **Text** (or **Paragraph**) | Optional reflections (e.g., “20 min meditation”). |

3. Set **Date** as the *default* value for new rows: click the column header, choose **Set as default**, and pick **Today**. This ensures each new entry automatically logs the current day.

### 2.3 Create a “Daily Log” view  

1. Add a new view → **Table** → name it *Daily Log*.  
2. Filter: **Date** → **Is today**.  
3. Group by **Habit** – this creates a separate section for each habit, making it easy to tick off multiple habits in one glance.

### 2.4 Automate a full‑day template  

Instead of adding each habit manually, use a **Template** that pre‑populates one row per habit for the current day:

1. Inside **Habit Tracker**, click **New → + New template**.  
2. Call it **Today’s Habits**.  
3. In the template page, add three **inline** table rows (click **+** inside the page, select **Table – Inline**).  
4. Populate the rows:  

| Habit | Date | Completed | Notes |
|-------|------|-----------|-------|
| Meditate | {{date}} | ☐ | |
| Exercise | {{date}} | ☐ | |
| Read | {{date}} | ☐ | |

5. Notion automatically replaces `{{date}}` with the date you choose when you create the page. Save the template.

Now, on any day, clicking **New → Today’s Habits** drops a ready‑made log where you simply check the boxes.

### 2.5 Visualize streaks with a calendar view  

1. Add another view → **Calendar** → *Habit Calendar*.  
2. In the calendar, each **Completed** checkbox appears as a colored dot (Notion automatically colors completed items).  
3. Use the **Group by** option → **Habit** to see separate mini‑calendars for each habit, revealing streaks at a glance.

## 3. Building a Personal Note‑Taking Vault  

### 3.1 Create the “Notes” database  

1. From the dashboard, click **+ New → Database → Table – Full page** and name it **Notes**.  
2. Add these properties:

| Property | Type | Purpose |
|----------|------|---------|
| **Tags** | **Multi‑select** (e.g., #research, #idea, #reference) | Enables flexible categorization. |
| **Source** | **Text** | Where the information came from (URL, book, etc.). |
| **Created** | **Created time** (auto‑filled) | Shows when the note was first added. |
| **Updated** | **Last edited time** (auto‑filled) | Tracks recent changes. |

The **Created time** and **Last edited time** are special property types that automatically capture timestamps—no manual entry needed.

### 3.2 Capture notes quickly with a template  

1. Inside **Notes**, click **New → + New template**.  
2. Name the template **Quick Capture**.  
3. In the template page, add a **heading** block titled **Key Insight** and a **bulleted list** block titled **Details / Quotes**.  
4. Add a **divider** and a **toggle** block labeled **Further Reading** where you can paste URLs or references later.  

Whenever inspiration strikes—during a meeting or while reading—you can jump to the **Notes** database, click **New → Quick Capture**, and start typing without worrying about formatting.

### 3.3 Organize with views  

1. **All Notes** – Default table view, sorted by **Created** descending.  
2. **By Tag** – New view → **Board** → *By Tag*. Group by **Tags** so each column represents a tag category. Drag notes between columns to retag them.  
3. **Recent** – New view → **Table** → *Recent*. Filter: **Updated** → **Is within the last** → **7** days. This surface‑shows notes you’ve been editing lately.

### 3.4 Link notes to tasks and habits  

Because Notion allows **Relations** (covered in *Introduction to Databases*), you can connect a note to a related task:

1. In the **Notes** database, add a property **Related Task** → **Relation** → select the **Tasks** database.  
2. When viewing a note, click the empty **Related Task** field, and pick the appropriate task.  
3. The selected task will now show a reciprocal link under a **Related Notes** column (you can rename it).  

Similarly, you could relate a habit entry to a note about a new workout routine, creating a web of context without leaving the page.

### 3. Offline capabilities and sync behavior  

#### What works offline?  

- Any page that you *have opened* at least once on the device stores a local copy.  
- **Blocks**, **databases**, and **templates** you edit while offline are saved locally and will appear exactly as you left them when you reconnect.  

#### How syncing happens  

1. **Edit while offline** – Notion writes changes to a local cache.  
2. **Re‑connect to the internet** – The app automatically syncs the cache with the cloud.  
3. **Conflict resolution** – If the same block was edited on another device while you were offline, Notion shows a **“Conflict”** banner, letting you choose which version to keep.  

#### Ensuring reliable offline access  

- **Open pages in advance** – Visit any page you anticipate needing before you lose connectivity (e.g., a travel itinerary before a flight).  
- **Use “Pin to Offline”** (available in Settings → **Offline** on iOS) to guarantee that a page stays cached even if you haven’t opened it recently.  
- **Check sync status** – The **top bar** displays a tiny cloud icon; a gray cloud means “offline”, while a blue cloud indicates a successful sync.

## Sharing a Page from Your Mobile Device  

You’ve just updated the *Weekend Getaway* page with a new hotel reservation and want to share it with your partner so they can add a note about activities. Here’s how to do it from the phone.  

### 1. Open the page you want to share

### 2. Tap the **Share** icon  

The paper‑plane icon in the top bar opens the **Sharing** dialog. This is the same place you clicked the **“Share”** button on the desktop, but optimized for touch.

| Method | When to use it | Steps |
|--------|----------------|-------|

## Glossary

**Block**: The fundamental unit of content in Notion, such as text, images, or embeds, that can be moved, edited, or nested.  

**Button Block**: A one‑click element that automates actions like creating a new page or database entry using a predefined template.  

**Database**: A structured collection of entries (rows) with defined properties (columns) that can be displayed in multiple view formats.  

**Filter**: A rule applied to a database view that hides rows not meeting specified criteria, helping surface relevant information.  

**Linked Database**: A synced copy of an existing database placed elsewhere, allowing you to view and filter the same data in a different context.  

**Page**: A standalone Notion document that can contain blocks, sub‑pages, and databases, serving as a primary building block of content.  

**Personal Dashboard**: A customized home‑base page that aggregates key information, shortcuts, and visual elements for quick access.  

**Property**: An attribute of a database entry, such as Title, Text, Select, Date, or Checkbox, that defines the type of data stored in a column.  

**Slash Command**: The “/” shortcut that opens a menu of block types, enabling quick insertion of text, databases, buttons, and more.  

**Sub‑Page**: A page nested within another page, allowing hierarchical organization of content and deeper detail without clutter.  

**Template**: A pre‑configured set of blocks and default property values that can be reused to speed up the creation of new pages or database entries.  

**View**: A specific presentation of a database (e.g., Board, Calendar, Table) that determines how entries are displayed and interacted with.  

**Workspace**: The top‑level container in Notion that groups related pages, databases, and members under a single shared environment.
